      G-9 AND G-13 LANDOWNERS’ INITIAL BRIEF ON ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13

       TO THE HONORABLE LINDA BRITE, DEE MARLO CHICO, AND LINDA J.

BURGESS          ADMINISTRATIVE             LAW       JUDGES           (ALJs),   STATE   OFFICE   OF

ADMINISTRATIVE HEARINGS (SOAH):

       COMES NOW, G-9 and G-13 Landowners, and files this Initial Brief in the above-styled

and numbered docket.

                                       I.    INTRODUCTION

       On September 18, 2026, the Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) remanded

this proceeding to SOAH on the basis that “the proposal for decision does not address all of the

issues identified in the March 30, 2026, preliminary order.”1 Specifically, the Commission found

the proposal for decision (PFD) did not provide recommendations on preliminary order issue

numbers 11 and 13.2 Preliminary order issue numbers 11 and 13 ask:




       1
           Order Remanding Proceeding to SOAH at 2 (Sept. 18, 2026).
       2
           Id.

                                                      2
        11.      Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal
                reliability standards?

       13.      What is the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result
                from the proposed transmission facilities considering both current and
                future expected congestion levels and the ability of the proposed
                transmission facilities to reduce those congestion levels?

       The ALJs, however, addressed these issues on pages 148-150 of the PFD.3 Specifically,

the ALJs addressed preliminary order issue number 11 through a finding that Oncor Electric

Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Service Corporation (collectively, Applicants)

presented the Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project (Project) as a project that will import power

from across Texas into the Permian Basin but did not assert that the transmission facilities were

necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards.4 Later, the Applicants asserted that Import

Path 2 is a reliability project.5 Based on this assertion, the ALJs determined that the analysis for

the cost to consumers and congested cost savings is not required, and as a result, noted that the

record does not contain evidence quantifying these savings.6

       The ALJs are correct in finding that the Applicants did not assert that the Project is

necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards and did not include evidence quantifying

the congested cost savings. However, the ALJs are incorrect in concluding that the analysis for

the cost to consumers and congestion cost savings was not required. Under Commission Rules for

new transmission line projects, there is a determination of need requirement.7 The Applicants

failed to meet this requirement. If the project is an economic project, then “[t]he applicant must




       3
           SOAH Proposal for Decision with Memorandum at 148-150 (Aug. 20, 2026) (Proposal for Decision).
       4
           Id. at 149.
       5
           Id. at 149-150 (citing App. Reply Br. at 24 (June 26, 2026) (“Import Path 2 is a reliability project . . . .”)).
       6
           Id. at 150.
       7
           16 Tex. Admin. Code (TAC) § 25.101.

                                                            3
 present an economic cost-benefit study that analyzes the transmission project under a congestion

cost savings test and a production cost savings test.”8 If the project is a reliability project that is

necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards, then the economic cost-benefit study is not

applicable.9 Here, Applicants failed to show that the Project is necessary to meet state or federal

reliability standards, so the economic cost-benefit study is applicable. As the record shows, and

the Applicants’ Directory of Record Evidence of Preliminary Order Issue Numbers 11 and 13

(Directory) confirms,10 Applicants failed to provide any evidence as to congestion cost savings

that may result from the proposed Project. Therefore, the Applicants failed to show need for the

Project as either a reliability project or an economic project. 11 As such, the ALJs’ ultimate

recommendation to deny the Application should be upheld.

                         II.    PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NUMBER 11

         In response to the Commission’s Remand Order, Applicants provided a Directory of

evidence addressing preliminary order issues 11 and 13.12 Applicants’ Directory included excerpts

from the record where preliminary order issue number 11 is addressed. Many of these excerpts

come from the Permian Basin Reliability Study and the 2024 and 2025 Regional Transmission

Plan.13 Based on the Directory, Applicants provided general information on the studies done



         8
              16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i).
         9
              16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(ii).
         10
            Applicants’ Directory of Evidence of Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13 (Sept. 21, 2026) (Applicants’
Directory of Evidence).
         11
             In addition to economic and reliability projects, 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(iii) states “ERCOT may
recommend, and the commission may approve, a transmission project that is submitted as an economic or reliability
project and does not demonstrate sufficient economic savings or reliability benefits to merit approval on those grounds
if ERCOT determines the line would address a resiliency issue identified in the grid reliability and resiliency
assessment required by subparagraph (E) of this paragraph.” Here, no party alleges that the Project would qualify as
a resiliency project under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(iii), and thus, this is not at issue or being addressed herein.
         12
              Applicants’ Directory of Evidence.
         13
              Id. at 3-15.

                                                          4
 showing import paths would be needed to transfer power to the Permian Basin.14 The Directory

further demonstrates that the Regional Transmission Plan (RTP) was conducted to satisfy the

North American Electric Reliability Corp (NERC) Standard, the ERCOT Planning Guide, and

ERCOT Nodal Protocols.15 However, nowhere do Applicants assert that this particular Project is

necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards. Instead, the Directory reflects general

statements regarding the need for the 765-kV transmission line projects to provide reliable service

to the Permian Basin.

       Nonetheless, if it were found that Applicants established that the Project is necessary to

meet state or federal reliability standards, the ALJs’ ultimate recommendation that the Application

be denied should be adopted. As the PFD asserts, there has been a change in circumstances leading

to a change in projected load in the Permian Basin which results in a lack of need for this Project.16

Some of these changed circumstances include changes in standards for large load customer

commitments,17 ERCOT’s adjusted load-forecasting methodology resulting in a 27% reduction to

the initial projected load forecast,18 the 2022 S&P Global Study (which the Permian Basin

Reliability Plan utilized to project the oil and gas demand) that projected 10.3 GW of oil and gas

by 2030 was significantly larger than ERCOT’s long-term forecasted 3.1 GW of oil and gas load,19

and planned generation in the Permian Basin.20 As a result, this Project is not necessary to provide

reliable service. Instead, a more affordable and less impactful project may be sufficient. Denial

 of the Application allows time to re-examine the actual projected load growth in the Permian Basin

and what generation or transmission projects would sufficiently and reliably meet that load growth.

Therefore, even if it was found that Applicants adequately showed the transmission facilities are

necessary to meet state and federal reliability standards, they are likely not needed due to a change

in the projected load growth.

                         III.   PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NUMBER 13

       The ALJs correctly concluded that the record contains no evidence quantifying either cost

to consumers or congestion cost savings.21 However, the ALJs’ determination that an analysis of

the cost to consumers and congestion cost savings was not required is incorrect. The Applicants’

failure to establish that the Project is necessary to meet state and federal reliability requirements

does not exempt it from having to perform economic tests for the Project. Since the Applicants

did not provide any evidence quantifying the cost to consumers or the congestion cost savings, the

Applicants did not establish need for the project pursuant to Commission Rules.22

       With respect to the Project’s congestion cost savings, the Applicants’ Directory contains

five pages of excerpts from the Application and testimony.23 Of these five pages, Applicants refer

to one chart from the RTP where it predicts congestion rent and the benefit of the 765-kV plan

versus the 365-kV plan.24 However, this chart shows the 765-kV plan as a whole and does not

specifically estimate the congestion cost savings for consumers that may result specifically from

this Project. Similarly, the only other “evidence” Applicants rely upon does not demonstrate the

estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from the proposed transmission

       22
            16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i).
       23

       24

                                                          6
 lines. Nor does it show the ability of the proposed transmission facilities’ ability to reduce

congestion levels. The Applicants’ own Directory confirms that Applicants failed to provide

evidence in support of preliminary order issue number 13. As such, the ALJs correctly found that

the record contains no evidence quantifying congestion cost savings because none was provided

by Applicants.

                                  IV.    CONCLUSION

       For the reasons stated above, the G-9 and G-13 Landowners respectfully requests the

Administrative Law Judges maintain their findings and continue to propose denial of the

Applicants’ Application. The G-9 and G-13 Landowners also request any such relief to which

they have shown themselves entitled.
